label: Institution
name: Baitul Awwal Mosque
summary:
Baitul Awwal Mosque, one of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community's mosque buildings, represents the global mosque-building program of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community — an Islamic movement founded in 1889 by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad in Qadian, India, which claims to be the reforming movement of Islam in the modern era but is considered heretical and non-Muslim by mainstream Sunni and Shia authorities, resulting in its members being officially declared non-Muslims in Pakistan (1974) and subject to severe persecution in Pakistan and parts of Indonesia.

The Ahmadiyya Muslim Community's global mosque-building program ('100 Mosques Campaign' and similar initiatives) has resulted in hundreds of mosques worldwide named with the 'Baitul' (House of) prefix — Baitul Awwal (First House), Baitul Futuh (House of Victories, the largest mosque in Western Europe, in London), etc. — as part of the community's systematic global expansion and its claim to represent true Islam.

The Ahmadiyya movement is historically significant in several ways: it was founded in British India during the late 19th-century Islamic reform movement, it has been the subject of the most sustained state-sanctioned religious persecution in the modern Islamic world (Pakistan's blasphemy laws making Ahmadi religious practice a criminal offense), and its global missionary activity has made it one of the fastest-growing Islamic movements internationally. The baitul mosques worldwide represent both a religious community's determination and the contested boundaries of Islamic identity.
